newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dlr slide is "dream come true" - wool exporters.
newsitem.headline: NZ dlr slide is "dream come true" - wool exporters.

text.p: A sudden fall in the New Zealand dollar against its U.S. counterpart and against sterling was "like a dream come true", wool exporters said on Friday.

After battling throughout the last season with a strong kiwi dollar dampening their price competitveness in the export-driven market, wool was now poised for a useful jump in its auction price in New Zealand when the new season starts on July 31.

"Exporters have had to absorb major stock valuation losses in the last two years, and carry the burden of contract defaults -- we'll be taking a pretty tough price line (this year)," Wool Exporters Council vice-president Kai Tovgaard said.

In a council market preview, Tovgaard said the dollar had devalued by 7.0 percent against the U.S. dollar and 11 percent against sterling, when compared to the average exchange rates for the 1996/97 season.
He called the move in the kiwi against the U.S. unit "realistic and long overdue".
Others in the export sector seemed to agree with the wool industry, as his comments were echoed by Dairy Board treasurer Geoff Taylor called the move a correction to an overvalued unit.

Tovgaard said the strength of the kiwi had little to do with the state of the New Zealand economy "and has ignored the fact that tour tiny population is almost wholly dependent on exports for its survival".
By today's New Zealand close the kiwi was trading at 0.6496/03, a full cent below its Thursday close of 0.6600/07.
The currency broke above 65 U.S. cents in mid-December 1995 and spent much of 1996 and early 1997 fairly close to 68 cents.
